description_full: PetroChina Company Limited, together with its subsidiaries, engages in a range of petroleum related products, services, and activities in Mainland China and internationally. It operates through the Oil and Gas and New Energy; Refining, Chemicals and New Materials; Sales; and Natural Gas Sales Segments. The Oil, Gas and New Energy Resource segment engages in the exploration, development, transportation, production, and marketing of crude oil and natural gas, as well as is involved in the new energy resource business. The Refining, Chemicals and New Materials segment refines crude oil and petroleum products; and produces and markets primary petrochemical products, derivative chemical products, and other chemical products; as well as engages in new materials business. The Sales segment is involved in the marketing of refined and non-oil products, and trading business. The Natural Gas Sales segment engages in the transmission and sale of natural gas. It is also involved in the exploration, development, and production of oil sands and coalbed methane; trading of crude oil and petrochemical products; investment in refining; storage, chemical engineering, storage facilities, service station, and transportation facilities and related businesses; chemical technology development; and provision of technology transfer and technical services. The company was incorporated in 1999 and is headquartered in Beijing, the People's Republic of China. PetroChina Company Limited operates as a subsidiary of China National Petroleum Corporation.

financial_summary: PetroChina Co., Ltd. is a mega-cap energy business with a $320.3B market cap on $482.3B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +10% over the past three years, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 5% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.

The business throws off $22.4B in free cash flow — roughly 5 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.40× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.3× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 10.1×.

Shareholder yield of 3.0% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

news_headlines.title: PetroChina (PCCYF) Expected to Post Earnings on Wednesday

sect: Its 7% operating margin trails the Energy median (16%) by 9pp, so it is a below-average operator in its field.
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.61x).
It accounts for 12.2% of sector revenue and 7.5% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-2.7% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.05 across 203 companies in the universe; the top four hold 40% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 12% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 18% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 54% and a beta of 0.33, it is more defensive than the market.
Trading is thin (about $20K a day), below the $1.0M liquidity floor flagged; building a position would move the price.
In past sell-offs it fell 43% in the 2020 crash, 29% in the 2022 bear market and 24% in 2008.
val: The stock trades only 14% below its DCF fair value of $1.51, a thin margin of safety.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 8%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $1.16 to $2.03 (P10-P90).
On multiples it looks cheap against Energy peers: P/E 8.7 vs 13.6 and EV/EBITDA 1.1 vs 7.1 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 111% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 7.0% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 6.0% (vs the 8% bar).
The price implies 6.1% annual cash-flow growth, 2pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 5% falls short of the cost of capital of 8.0%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.53).
It converts 5% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 7/9 and cash conversion of 2.40x.
ROE of 12% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.0x equity multiplier).
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 0.3x net debt to EBITDA ($27.5B of cash against $37.5B of debt), with interest covered 10.1x.
The current ratio of 0.98 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 9.8% over 3 years and 10.1% over 5 years, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 22%).
Free cash flow has compounded 1.9% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
own: Insiders own a modest 1.5%, and institutions hold 31%.
It returns 3.0% a year to shareholders (6.2% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 12 consecutive years, raising it 16.6% a year over the last five.
people: With about 367,173 employees, each generates about $1.3M of revenue, 0.6x the Energy median, and revenue has grown 10.1% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $61K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $155K (0x revenue per employee).
